summary:
We developed the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. This is a browser based survival game for children between seven and twelve years old. Players take on the role of a Junior Commander at a base on Mars or the Moon and manage important resources like power, oxygen and water.

In doing so they overcome authentic environmental hazards. The special thing about this is that all tasks come from real missions such as the Apollo 13 emergency repairs or the Perseverance rover oxygen extraction. We transformed complex NASA data into intuitive minigames. Players repair broken cables, survive sandstorms and manage technological upgrades under strict time pressure. If a base fails a detailed analysis at the end shows the exact physical reason for it so players can learn from their mistakes.

This project is extremely important because it builds a bridge between real science and interactive education. It inspires children to abandon their Euclidean understanding and become even more enthusiastic about space. By experiencing the thrill of real space exploration firsthand and learning from real physics this is exactly how the next great figures in spaceflight are inspired.
details:
What does it do or how does it work? Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a 2D side-scrolling, browser-based survival simulation designed for children aged 7–12. Players take on the role of a Junior Commander managing either a Martian or Lunar outpost. They must balance critical resources like battery power, oxygen, and water while managing a pressurized rover and an expandable base. The core gameplay loop requires players to survive authentic environmental hazards—such as wind-driven Martian dust storms or sudden Lunar Solar Particle Events (SPE)—by manually securing base systems and rationing EVA (Extravehicular Activity) time.

How is your project creative and what factors did your team consider? To make complex aerospace engineering accessible to young minds, we completely eliminated traditional UI buttons from our minigames. Instead, we implemented "buttonless" visual drag-and-drop mechanics. For example, players physically drag a roll of duct tape to seal a leaking pipe or carefully pull a lever to keep the MOXIE reactor exactly between 780–820 °C. We also factored in the attention span of our target audience by replacing text-heavy instructions with a playable, AAA-style prologue tutorial that safely teaches mechanics before launching a scripted, planet-specific crisis. Visually, we adopted a minimalist, crisp 2.5D aesthetic with distinct planetary biomes (blue sunsets on Mars vs. pitch-black starry skies on the Moon).

What is the intended impact of the project? The project aims to build a bridge between real science and interactive education. By hiding complex NASA telemetry (like 0.6 kPa Mars atmospheric pressure, or 0.84 kg daily O2 consumption) behind intuitive gameplay, it inspires children to abandon rigid Euclidean learning in favor of hands-on, experiential physics. Detailed post-game analyses explain exactly why a base failed using real physical constraints, inspiring the next generation of spaceflight innovators.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use? The game was developed entirely using native Web Technologies: HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript. We utilized the HTML5 Canvas API to render the parallax environments, weather particle systems (sandstorms), and custom animations. We also leveraged Super Intelligence (SI) tools for rapid prototyping, logic troubleshooting, and code generation.
dataRefs: NASA Mars Fact Sheet (Used for gravity, atmospheric pressure of 0.6 kPa, and Sol length)
NASA Mars 2020 MOXIE Instrument (Used for the 800°C oxygen extraction minigame)
NASA Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS)
NASA Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (BVAD - Used for 0.84kg O2 daily consumption math)
projectRefs: Anthropic Claude (Used for JavaScript Canvas code generation and debugging)
